genZNote: The single most common cause of tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) in kids in much of the world — it invades the hair shaft from the inside out (endothrix).

morphology.arrangement: Branching septate hyphae with microconidia along the hyphae

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human skin and hair (anthropophilic — adapted specifically to humans)
habitat.hostAssociation: Exclusively infects humans; spread via direct contact or shared fomites (combs, hats, pillows)
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Can persist on fomites for extended periods, facilitating spread in households and schools
habitat.reservoir: Infected humans and contaminated personal items

microscopy.appearance: Endothrix arrangement — arthroconidia packed inside the hair shaft, not on its surface
microscopy.arrangement: Septate hyphae fragmenting into arthroconidia within the hair

culture.growthCharacteristics: Slow-growing mold, 1-2+ weeks for mature colonies
culture.colonyMorphology: Suede-like to powdery, tan-brown to yellow colonies with a reddish-brown reverse pigment

identificationClues: Endothrix pattern of hair invasion (arthroconidia packed inside the hair shaft) seen on microscopy — the key feature distinguishing it from ectothrix dermatophytes like Microsporum canis
The leading cause of tinea capitis in many regions, especially among school-age children, often presenting with 'black dot' alopecia patches
Anthropophilic — transmitted human-to-human or via shared combs/hats/pillows rather than from animals
Does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp, unlike most Microsporum species — an important clinical bedside distinction

clinicalImportance.transmission: Direct person-to-person contact or via shared fomites (combs, hats, pillows, barber tools)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most common causes of tinea capitis worldwide, particularly prevalent among children in urban settings
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Endothrix hair invasion pattern and lack of Wood's lamp fluorescence distinguish it from Microsporum-caused tinea capitis

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — identified by microscopy/culture morphology
examFacts.importantDisease: Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm), especially in children
examFacts.importantTest: KOH prep showing endothrix hair invasion; no Wood's lamp fluorescence
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Leading anthropophilic cause of tinea capitis with endothrix hair invasion, unlike the ectothrix, fluorescent Microsporum canis
